stories.title: God makes the world
stories.drawPrompt: Color the sky, the sea, and the land. Draw one more thing God made.

activity.prompt: What did God do on the seventh day?
activity.explanation: God rested from the work of creation and set the seventh day apart.

paragraphs: At the beginning, darkness lay over deep water. God spoke, and there was light. God called the light day and the darkness night. The first evening and morning passed.
God made the sky. Then God gathered the waters so dry ground could appear. God named the dry ground land and the waters seas. Soon the land grew plants and trees with fruit.

God made lights for the sky, creatures to swim in the water, and birds to fly above the land. Then came animals that lived on land. God made people in his own image and gave them a world full of life to care for.
God looked at everything he had made and called it very good. When the work was finished, God rested. He blessed the seventh day and set it apart.
young.question: Which part of the world in this story would you like to explore? How could you take care of it?

paragraphs: Genesis begins with God creating the heavens and the earth. At first the earth is unformed, darkness covers the deep, and God’s Spirit moves over the waters. God calls light into being and gives names to the light and the darkness.

God separates waters to make the sky. The waters below gather into seas so dry ground can appear. The ground grows plants that produce seed and trees that bear fruit. These early scenes give the world places where life can grow.

Lights mark the passage of time. Fish and other creatures fill the waters, birds fill the sky, and animals live on land. God makes human beings in his image, blesses them, and gives them responsibility for the living world.
The repeated words that creation is good build toward God calling everything very good. The seventh day has a different purpose. God finishes the work, rests, and blesses that day.
middle.question: What responsibilities go with being given a world that God calls good?

paragraphs: Genesis opens with darkness and a watery deep. God’s speech begins ordering that world. Watch for the repeated sequence of God speaking, something happening, and God looking at the result. The repetitions help readers follow the movement of the chapter.

The first three days describe light and darkness, waters and sky, then land, seas, and vegetation. Notice how the next three days return to those spaces in order. The passage uses that structure to draw attention to the relationships among the parts of creation.

Days four through six fill the ordered world with lights and living creatures. The account slows down when God makes humanity. Both male and female bear God’s image. The blessing and charge that follow connect that identity with responsibility for the rest of creation.
Genesis 2:1–3 closes the sequence with God blessing a day. The culmination of the work is rest. Read the final verses alongside Genesis 1:31 and consider what the text treats as the goal of the work.
teen.question: How do the words image, good, and rest shape what this passage says about a human life?

middle: Fold or tape together seven panels.
Pair the first three panels with the next three. Mark the connections between light and lights, sky and water and their creatures, and land and its creatures.
Add a seventh panel for rest and explain what it contributes to the story.
teen: Turn seven folded panels into a visual outline of Genesis 1:1–2:3.
Add a brief verse citation for each image and use matching colors to connect related days.
Use the final panel to show how the seventh day differs from the others.

stories.title: Joseph and his brothers
scenes: A plan for the years of hunger
stories.drawPrompt: Give Joseph’s coat bright stripes. Choose a different color for each stripe.

activity.prompt: Why did Joseph’s brothers go to Egypt?
activity.explanation: There was a famine at home, and Egypt had grain because Joseph had stored it.

paragraphs: Joseph’s father gave him a special coat. Joseph also had dreams in which his family bowed to him. His brothers grew jealous. One day, far from home, they threw him into a pit and sold him to traders.

The traders took Joseph to Egypt. He worked in another man’s house and later ended up in prison after someone accused him of something he had not done. While there, Joseph helped two prisoners understand their dreams.

When Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, had strange dreams, Joseph explained their meaning. Years of good harvests would be followed by years with little food. Pharaoh put Joseph in charge of storing grain while there was plenty.

During the famine, Joseph’s brothers came to Egypt to buy grain. They did not recognize him at first. Later Joseph told them who he was. He wept, embraced them, and asked them to bring their father to Egypt, where the family could have food.
young.question: What do you notice about how Joseph treated his brothers when he could have sent them away?

paragraphs: Jacob gave Joseph a special robe, and his brothers saw how much their father favored him. When Joseph shared his dreams of the family bowing to him, their anger grew. One day they dropped Joseph into an empty pit. He was sold to traders, and the brothers let Jacob believe he was dead.

In Egypt Joseph served in Potiphar’s household. After a false accusation, he was imprisoned. Two of Pharaoh’s officials had dreams there. Joseph told them that God could give the meanings, and the events happened as he said. The cupbearer was restored to his job and forgot Joseph for a time.

Pharaoh later dreamed of seven thin cows swallowing seven healthy ones and seven thin heads of grain swallowing good grain. Joseph explained that seven years of plenty would be followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh placed him over the work of collecting and storing food.

Joseph recognized his brothers when they came for grain. After several meetings, he saw Judah offer to take Benjamin’s place as a servant. Joseph sent the other people out of the room, wept, and said who he was. He told his brothers to bring their father to Egypt so the family could survive the famine.
middle.question: What does Judah’s offer to take Benjamin’s place show about the way he has changed?

paragraphs: Genesis 37 shows jealousy growing inside a family. Jacob’s favor, the robe, and Joseph’s dreams become part of the brothers’ anger. Reuben speaks against killing Joseph, while Judah proposes selling him. Keep their choices in view when the brothers have to decide what to do about Benjamin later.

Joseph’s position changes more than once in Egypt. A trusted servant becomes a prisoner after a false accusation. In prison, he credits God with the interpretation of dreams. The cupbearer’s delay leaves Joseph waiting even after an interpretation has proved true.

In Genesis 41, Joseph interprets Pharaoh’s two dreams as one message and proposes a response. Grain must be gathered during the years of plenty if people are to survive the famine. The story connects Joseph’s ability to interpret the dreams with the practical work of planning ahead.

Judah’s speech in Genesis 44 offers himself in place of Benjamin and recalls what another loss would do to Jacob. In Genesis 45 Joseph identifies himself and speaks of God preserving life. Read his words alongside the brothers’ earlier actions and consider how the story holds harm, responsibility, and forgiveness together.
teen.question: What evidence does Genesis give that Judah has changed, and what does Joseph do with the power he now has?

stories.title: Ruth stays with Naomi
stories.drawPrompt: Color the barley that Ruth gathers. Draw a basket for the grain she brings home.

activity.prompt: How did Ruth find food for herself and Naomi?
options: She gathered grain left by workers
She baked bread for the town
activity.explanation: Ruth gathered leftover grain in Boaz’s field and brought it home to Naomi.

paragraphs: Naomi’s family had left Bethlehem when food was scarce and moved to Moab. Naomi’s husband and sons died there. When she heard that there was food in Bethlehem again, she decided to go home.
Naomi told her daughters-in-law, Ruth and Orpah, that they could stay in Moab. Orpah said goodbye. Ruth stayed with Naomi and promised to go where she went and to worship her God.

In Bethlehem, Ruth gathered grain the harvest workers had left behind. The field belonged to Boaz. When he learned how Ruth had cared for Naomi, he invited her to gather grain safely there and gave her food to eat.
Ruth took her grain and some food she had saved to Naomi. She kept working through the harvest. Later Boaz and Ruth married. They had a son named Obed, and Naomi helped care for him.
young.question: What is one thing Ruth or Boaz did that you could do in your own way to help someone?

paragraphs: A famine took Naomi, her husband, and their sons from Bethlehem to Moab. After Naomi lost her husband and both sons, she heard that food was available in Judah again. She started home with her daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth.

Naomi urged the women to return to their families. Orpah kissed her goodbye. Ruth held on to Naomi and promised to share her journey, her people, and her God. They reached Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Ruth went to glean, which meant picking up grain the harvesters left behind. She came to a field belonging to Boaz, a relative of Naomi’s family. Boaz told his workers to keep her safe, invited her to eat, and asked the workers to leave extra grain for her.

Ruth and Naomi had help through the harvest. Boaz later spoke to a nearer relative and the town elders before agreeing to marry Ruth. Their son Obed became the grandfather of David. The women of Bethlehem celebrated with Naomi.
middle.question: How did Boaz help Ruth keep working and providing for Naomi?

paragraphs: The book begins with hunger, migration, and loss. Naomi’s return comes after she hears that food is available in Judah. The opening also makes clear that Ruth begins this journey as a Moabite woman with a future she has to choose.

Orpah returns after Naomi’s urging. Ruth binds herself to Naomi, to her people, and to her God. The women arrive at harvest, a detail that sets up the field scenes and stands in contrast to the famine that began the story.

Ruth goes out to glean. The field belongs to Boaz, who asks about her, recognizes what she has done for Naomi, and tells the men to leave her alone and leave her extra grain. Notice how safety, food, and work all matter to the kindness of this scene.

At the town gate, Boaz resolves the question of the nearer relative before he marries Ruth. The closing scene draws attention to Naomi caring for Obed and continues into a genealogy ending with David. Read how far the book has traveled from Naomi’s first return to Bethlehem.
teen.question: What makes kindness in Ruth practical, and what would that kind of support look like in a community today?

stories.title: Jesus feeds the five thousand
stories.drawPrompt: Color the bread and fish. Draw another basket for the food left over.

activity.prompt: How many baskets of pieces were left after everyone ate?
activity.explanation: The disciples filled twelve baskets with pieces left over from the five barley loaves.

paragraphs: Jesus went up a hillside near the Sea of Galilee. A big crowd followed because they had seen him heal people. When Jesus looked up and saw them coming, he asked his friend Philip where they could get bread for everyone.
Philip thought even a great deal of money would not buy enough. Another friend, Andrew, found a boy with five barley loaves and two fish. Andrew wondered how so little could feed all those people.
Jesus asked the people to sit on the grass. He took the bread and gave thanks to God. Then he shared the bread and fish. Everyone had as much as they wanted.
When everyone had eaten, Jesus asked his friends to collect the pieces so they would not be wasted. They filled twelve baskets. They had started with a little meal, and now there was food left over.
young.question: What would you have noticed when the baskets came back full?

paragraphs: A crowd crossed toward Jesus near the Sea of Galilee after seeing his signs of healing. John mentions that Passover was near. Jesus sat on a hillside with his disciples and asked Philip where they could buy enough bread for the crowd.

Philip calculated that even two hundred denarii would not buy enough for everyone to have a little. Andrew pointed out a boy with five barley loaves and two fish. The disciples could see both the food in front of them and how large the crowd was.
Jesus asked everyone to sit in the grassy place. John says there were about five thousand men. Jesus gave thanks and distributed bread and fish to the people, who ate as much as they wanted.

At Jesus’ direction, the disciples gathered the leftover pieces and filled twelve baskets. The people called Jesus the Prophet they were expecting. When Jesus realized they meant to take him and make him king, he withdrew to the mountain alone.
middle.question: How do Philip’s estimate and the twelve baskets help tell the story from beginning to end?

paragraphs: John 6 places the feeding near Passover and describes a crowd drawn by Jesus’ signs of healing. Jesus asks Philip about buying bread. John tells readers that Jesus already knows what he will do, making the question an invitation to see how the disciples understand the need.

Philip thinks about wages and cost. Andrew names a boy’s five barley loaves and two fish while admitting their smallness compared with the crowd. The ordinary details prepare the reader to notice how the outcome differs from what either disciple expects.

Jesus has the people sit, gives thanks, and distributes food. Everyone can eat until satisfied. He then tells the disciples to gather the fragments. John records both the abundance and Jesus’ desire that the remaining bread be collected.

The crowd calls Jesus the Prophet and wants to make him king. Jesus withdraws. Later he speaks about bread that lasts and calls himself the bread of life. The feeding meets a real hunger and opens a conversation about what the crowd is seeking from him.
teen.question: How does the conversation in John 6:26–35 change what you notice in the feeding story?

stories.title: Jesus is risen
stories.drawPrompt: Color the empty tomb. Draw the morning sun above the stone that was rolled away.

activity.prompt: What news did the angel tell the women?
options: Jesus was still in the tomb
They should go back the next day
activity.explanation: The angel said that Jesus had risen and told the women to share the news with his disciples.

paragraphs: After Jesus died, his body was placed in a tomb with a large stone across its doorway. Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and another woman named Mary came to see the tomb.
The ground shook, and an angel rolled the stone away and sat on it. The guards were very afraid. The angel told the women they could come and see the place where Jesus had been. Jesus had risen.
The angel asked the women to tell Jesus’ friends that he was alive and would meet them in Galilee. The women hurried away. They were afraid and full of joy at the same time.
On the way, Jesus met them and greeted them. The women held his feet and worshiped him. Jesus told them not to be afraid and asked them again to carry the news to his friends.
young.question: How do you think the women felt when they saw Jesus on the way?

paragraphs: After Jesus’ death, Joseph of Arimathea placed his body in a new tomb cut from rock and rolled a great stone across the entrance. Matthew says the tomb was secured and guarded. At dawn after the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see it.

A strong earthquake accompanied the arrival of an angel. The angel rolled the stone back and sat on it. The guards shook with fear. The angel told the women not to be afraid and invited them to see where Jesus had lain.
The angel said Jesus had risen, as he had told them he would. The women were to tell the disciples that Jesus was going ahead of them to Galilee. They left in a hurry with fear and great joy.
Jesus himself met the women before they reached the disciples. They took hold of his feet and worshiped him. Jesus repeated the message about Galilee and called the disciples his brothers.
middle.question: How is meeting Jesus on the road different from hearing the angel’s message at the tomb?

paragraphs: Read Matthew’s burial account alongside the resurrection scene. At the burial, the two Marys watch across from the tomb. When the story returns to them, they go to the same place, now guarded and sealed. Matthew uses the continuity to connect the death, burial, and discovery.

The angel rolls the stone away and sits on it. The guards shake, while the women hear the command not to fear. They are invited to see the empty place and to understand it in light of what Jesus had already said.

The women are sent from the tomb toward the disciples with news that Jesus will meet them in Galilee. Matthew describes them as afraid and joyful at once. Their response is to go and carry the message they have heard.

Before they reach the others, the women meet Jesus himself and worship him. He repeats the commission, calling the disciples his brothers. Consider how the story moves from seeking a tomb to being sent out with news of someone they have met.
teen.question: What changes between the women’s visit to the tomb and their meeting with Jesus, and why does Matthew include both scenes?

stories.title: Noah and the ark
stories.drawPrompt: Color the ark, the animals, and the rainbow. Draw a dove carrying a leaf nearby.

activity.prompt: What did the dove bring back to Noah?
activity.explanation: The olive leaf helped Noah see that the water was going down.

paragraphs: People on earth were hurting one another. God told Noah a flood was coming and showed him how to build a huge boat called an ark. Noah built it with rooms inside and covered it to keep the water out.
Noah, his family, and the animals went into the ark. They brought food for the people and the animals. When they were inside, God shut the door.
Rain fell for forty days and nights. The waters rose and lifted the ark off the ground. Later the rain stopped, and the water slowly went down. The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.

Noah sent out a dove, but it came back because it could not find a place to rest. After seven days he tried again. This time the dove carried back a fresh olive leaf. Noah knew the water was going down.

When God told Noah to leave the ark, his family and the animals went out onto dry ground. God promised that a flood would never again destroy all life on earth. He put a rainbow in the clouds as a sign of his promise.
young.question: What sign did God give Noah and his family?

paragraphs: Genesis says the earth was full of violence. God warned Noah of the flood and gave him directions for building a wooden ark. Noah was to put rooms and decks inside, coat the ark with pitch, and collect enough food for the people and animals it would shelter.

Noah’s wife, his three sons, and their wives went aboard with him. Animals and birds came into the ark as God had directed. Genesis ends the boarding scene with a detail about who closed the door. The Lord shut Noah in.

Rain fell for forty days and nights, and the ark rose with the water. After many days, God sent a wind and the waters began to recede. The ark rested in the mountains of Ararat, but Noah still had to wait for dry ground.

Noah opened the ark’s window and sent out birds. The dove returned the first time without finding a resting place. After seven days it returned with a fresh olive leaf. Noah waited another seven days, and the dove did not come back the third time.

God told Noah to bring his family and the animals out. Noah built an altar and worshiped. God made a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature. The rainbow would be a sign of the promise that a flood would never again destroy all flesh.
middle.question: Who is included in God’s promise in Genesis 9:8–17?

paragraphs: Genesis 6 describes an earth corrupted by violence. Noah receives instructions to build an ark with specific dimensions, decks, a door, and pitch inside and out. The work of preparing shelter and storing provisions gives the story a practical dimension before the flood arrives.

The people boarding the ark are Noah, his wife, their sons, and their sons’ wives. The animals are brought in under God’s directions. The narrative records Noah’s obedience and then closes the scene by naming the Lord as the one who shuts him in.

The flood is measured in stages. Forty days of rain lift the ark, and the waters prevail for much longer. Genesis 8 begins its reversal by saying that God remembered Noah and the creatures in the ark. A wind passes over the earth, and the waters begin to recede.

Noah’s three releases of the dove measure what he can know from inside the ark. The bird returns with no resting place, later returns with an olive leaf, and finally stays away. Even after Noah sees the ground drying, he leaves when God gives the instruction.

Noah’s first action outside the ark is worship. God’s covenant in Genesis 9 expressly reaches Noah’s descendants and other creatures. The rainbow marks a promise about the preservation of life as the story closes, after an opening that emphasized the destruction human violence had brought.
teen.question: How does the scope of the covenant in Genesis 9 change how you read the opening of the flood story?

stories.title: Jesus calms the storm
stories.drawPrompt: Color the boat and the waves. Draw a patch of calm water where the storm has passed.

activity.prompt: What did Jesus do when his friends woke him?
options: He spoke to the wind and waves
activity.explanation: Jesus spoke to the wind and waves, and the storm became calm.

paragraphs: Jesus had been teaching beside the Sea of Galilee. That evening he told his friends they would cross to the other side. They left the crowd behind and took Jesus with them in the boat.

A strong wind came up on the lake. Waves splashed over the sides and the boat began to fill with water. Jesus was asleep on a cushion at the back of the boat. His friends woke him and asked if he cared that they were in danger.
Jesus got up and spoke to the wind and the waves. He told them to be still. The wind stopped and the lake became quiet.
Jesus asked his friends why they were afraid and where their faith was. They were amazed. They asked one another who Jesus could be, since even the wind and the waves listened to him.
young.question: What did Jesus’ friends do when the storm scared them?

paragraphs: After teaching a crowd from a boat, Jesus told the disciples to cross the lake that evening. They left the crowd behind and took him as he was. Mark also notes that other boats went with them.

As they crossed, a fierce windstorm drove waves into the boat. The disciples found Jesus asleep on a cushion in the stern, the back of the boat. They woke him with a question about whether he cared that they might drown.
Jesus stood up and rebuked the wind. He told the sea to be still. The wind died away, and the violent water became very calm.

Jesus asked the disciples why they were afraid and whether they still lacked faith. They were filled with fear after the storm had stopped and asked one another who he was. The danger had gone, but the question about Jesus grew larger.
middle.question: How do the disciples’ questions change from the beginning of the storm to the end?

paragraphs: In Mark 4, a day of teaching beside the sea leads into a night crossing. Jesus initiates the trip. Mark’s references to evening, other boats, and a cushion in the stern keep the scene grounded in the details of an ordinary journey.

The storm threatens to fill the boat while Jesus sleeps. The disciples ask him whether he cares that they are perishing. Their words make a question about Jesus’ care part of a situation that is already physically dangerous.

Jesus rebukes the wind and addresses the sea. Mark moves from a great windstorm to a great calm. Psalm 107:23–30 describes sailors calling on the Lord in a storm and offers a comparison for the way Mark presents the stilling of the sea.

After the calm, Jesus asks about fear and faith. The disciples’ great fear then becomes a question of identity. Read their final question next to their first question and notice how the same people move from asking about care to asking who Jesus is.
teen.question: What do the two questions the disciples ask reveal about what they still have to learn?

activity.prompt: How did the Samaritan help the traveler?
options: He told him to stand up
He cared for him and took him to an inn
activity.explanation: The Samaritan stayed with the wounded traveler and made sure someone would look after him.

paragraphs: A man asked Jesus who counted as his neighbor. Jesus began a story about a traveler taking the road from Jerusalem down to Jericho. Robbers hurt the traveler and left him by the road.
A priest came down the road. He saw the hurt traveler and went by on the other side. A Levite, another person who served at the temple, came along and did the same thing.
A Samaritan saw the traveler and stopped. He treated the man’s wounds and helped him onto his animal. Then he took him to an inn and cared for him.

The next day the Samaritan paid the innkeeper to keep looking after the traveler. Jesus asked which person had been a neighbor to the man. The answer was the person who showed mercy. Jesus told the man to go and do the same.
young.question: What is one kind thing you could do for someone who needs help?

paragraphs: An expert in the law asked Jesus about eternal life. When Jesus asked what the law said, the man answered that he should love God and love his neighbor. Then he asked who his neighbor was. Jesus replied with a story about the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.

Robbers stripped and beat a traveler, leaving him badly hurt. A priest saw the man and crossed to the other side. A Levite came to the place and passed by too. The story describes what they saw and did without explaining why they kept going.
A Samaritan came near and felt compassion. He treated the traveler’s wounds with oil and wine and bandaged them. He put the traveler on his own animal, took him to an inn, and cared for him there.

The next day the Samaritan gave the innkeeper two coins and promised to pay more if care cost more. Jesus asked who acted like a neighbor to the man. When the expert answered that it was the one who showed mercy, Jesus asked him to do likewise.
middle.question: What did it cost the Samaritan to stop and help?

paragraphs: The conversation in Luke 10 begins with an expert in the law asking about eternal life. Jesus returns the question to what he reads in the law. The expert names love of God and of neighbor, then asks who his neighbor is. The parable answers that second question.

A traveler going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is robbed, beaten, and left in need of help. The priest and Levite both see him and pass by. Their motives are left unstated, which makes their observable choices the focus of this part of the story.

The Samaritan sees the same person and has compassion. The narrative spends time on each action: treating wounds, transporting the traveler, taking him to shelter, and caring for him overnight. In the world of the story, the Samaritan is the person the questioner might least expect to act as the neighbor.

The Samaritan pays for continued care and agrees to cover the rest. Jesus asks who became a neighbor to the injured man. The expert identifies the one who showed mercy. The shift from defining a neighbor to becoming a neighbor leads directly to Jesus’ instruction to act.
teen.question: How would a real situation change if you asked how to become a neighbor to someone instead of asking whether they count as one?

activity.prompt: How did Jesus respond when people brought children to him?
options: He told them to wait outside
He asked them to come back when they were older
activity.explanation: Jesus welcomed the children, took them in his arms, and blessed them.

paragraphs: People came to Jesus and brought children with them. They hoped Jesus would lay his hands on the children and bless them.
Jesus’ friends told the people to stop. When Jesus saw what was happening, he was upset and told his friends to let the children come.
Jesus said that God’s kingdom belongs to people like these children. He told the people listening that they must receive the kingdom like a child.
Then Jesus took the children in his arms. He put his hands on them and blessed them. The children the disciples had tried to turn away were right beside him.
young.question: How can you make someone feel welcome today?

paragraphs: People brought children to Jesus to ask for his blessing. Mark says they wanted Jesus to touch them. Matthew, who also tells the story, says they wanted him to put his hands on the children and pray.
The disciples scolded the people who brought the children. Jesus saw it and was upset. He told his disciples to let the children come and to stop getting in their way.

Jesus said the kingdom of God belongs to people like the children. He went on to say that anyone who does not receive God’s kingdom like a child will not enter it. The children became the center of a lesson for the adults.
Jesus took the children into his arms, placed his hands on them, and blessed them. His welcome included what he did as well as what he said.
middle.question: What do Jesus’ words and actions show about who matters to him?

paragraphs: Mark gives a short account with a clear sequence. People bring children so Jesus might touch them, the disciples rebuke the people, and Jesus sees what has happened. Pay attention to who acts and who is spoken to at each point.

Jesus is indignant and tells the disciples to let the children come. The disciples’ attempt to manage access is part of the story because Jesus addresses it directly. His words make room for the children the disciples had tried to turn away.

Jesus links the children to the kingdom of God. He says it belongs to people like them and must be received like a child. Mark gives no list of childhood qualities, leaving readers to consider what receiving a gift means in this scene.

The passage ends with Jesus taking the children into his arms, laying his hands on them, and blessing them. The children become recipients of attention and care as well as the people through whom the disciples learn.
teen.question: Where do people your age get overlooked, and how does Jesus’ response shape what you might do?

activity.prompt: What did the father do when he saw his son coming home?
activity.explanation: The father saw his son from far away, ran to him, and hugged him.

paragraphs: Jesus told a story about a father with two sons. The younger son asked for his share of the family’s things. After his father divided what he owned, the son took his share far away and spent it.

When the land ran short of food, the son took a job feeding pigs. He was so hungry he wanted what the pigs were eating. He thought about home, where his father’s workers had bread, and decided to go back and say he was sorry.
The father saw him far down the road. He ran to hug him. The son said he had done wrong, and his father called for a robe, a ring, and a meal to celebrate. His son had come home.

The older son heard music and was angry when he learned why there was a party. His father came outside to talk to him. He told him there was reason to be glad because his brother had been lost and was found.
young.question: How do you think the son felt when his father ran to hug him?

paragraphs: Jesus tells of a father with two sons. The younger asks for his inheritance before his father dies. The father divides his property, and the younger son takes his share to a far country, where he spends what he has.

A famine comes when the money is gone. The son takes work feeding pigs and is hungry enough to want their food. He remembers his father’s workers have bread to spare. He plans to go home, confess what he did, and ask to be treated as a worker.

The father sees his son from far away and runs to embrace him. The son says he has sinned and is unworthy to be called a son. The father calls for the best robe, a ring, sandals, and a celebration for the son he thought was lost.

The older son comes back from the fields and refuses to go inside. He tells his father why the party seems unfair. The father goes out to him too, says all he has is already his, and asks him to be glad that his brother is alive and home.
middle.question: What does the father do to welcome each of his sons?

paragraphs: Luke 15 begins with complaints that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. The parable introduces a father who divides his property between two sons. The younger son leaves and spends his share in a distant place.

The famine exposes how little the younger son has left. While feeding pigs, he remembers food in his father’s house and rehearses a confession and a request to become a hired worker. Notice what he expects he will have to ask for on his return.

Before the younger son reaches the house, his father sees him, runs, and embraces him. The son confesses, and the father calls for signs of welcome and a feast. The anticipated conversation about a hired worker gives way to a public celebration of his return as a son.

The father also goes out to the older brother, who speaks of his years of service and the unfairness he feels. The father affirms their relationship and asks him to share the joy. Luke leaves the older brother’s response open to the listener.
teen.question: Which brother is harder for you to understand, and how does the father respond to him?

paragraphs: David brought food to his brothers, who were with Israel’s army. From the other side of the valley, a giant soldier named Goliath challenged someone to fight him. The soldiers were afraid, but David told King Saul he would go.

David remembered how God had helped him protect his sheep. Saul offered David armor, but David was not used to wearing it. He put it aside, picked five smooth stones from a stream, and took his sling.

Goliath laughed when he saw David. David said that the battle belonged to the Lord. He slung a stone that struck Goliath, and Goliath fell. The shepherd boy had faced the soldier everyone was afraid of.
young.question: What did David remember when he needed courage?

paragraphs: Goliath repeated his challenge for forty days while the armies faced each other across a valley. David arrived with supplies from home and heard the challenge for himself. When he volunteered, Saul pointed out the difference between a young shepherd and a soldier who had trained for years.

David recalled defending his sheep from a lion and a bear and said the Lord who rescued him then could rescue him again. He tried Saul’s armor and found he could not move easily in it. He went down with his own staff, sling, and five stones from the stream.

Goliath mocked David’s size and equipment. David answered that the Lord did not need a sword or spear to save. One stone brought Goliath down. The narrator emphasizes that David prevailed with a sling and a stone before he had a sword in his hand.

activity.prompt: Where did God send Jonah?
activity.explanation: God sent Jonah to warn the people of Nineveh.

paragraphs: God told Jonah to go to Nineveh and warn the people there. Jonah got on a ship going the other way. A strong storm hit the ship. Jonah told the sailors to put him in the sea, and the storm stopped.
God sent a great fish that swallowed Jonah. Jonah prayed inside the fish. After three days and nights, God told the fish to put Jonah back on dry land.
God gave Jonah his job again, and this time Jonah went to Nineveh. The people listened to his warning and turned away from the wrong things they were doing. God spared their city.
Jonah was angry. Outside the city, he was glad when a plant gave him shade, and sad when it dried up. God asked Jonah why God should not care about a whole city full of people and animals.
young.question: Who got a second chance in this story?

paragraphs: Jonah boarded a ship for Tarshish after God told him to go to Nineveh. When a storm threatened the ship, Jonah admitted he was running away and told the sailors to throw him overboard. They first tried rowing to land. When they finally put him in the sea, the water grew calm.
God appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah. Jonah’s prayer remembers sinking deep in the water and thanks God for bringing him up from danger. After three days and nights, the fish put Jonah ashore.

The second time God called, Jonah went to Nineveh and announced that the city would be overthrown in forty days. From the king down, people humbled themselves and turned away from violence. When God saw what they did, he spared the city.

Jonah said he had fled because he knew God was merciful. He sat outside the city, where a plant shaded him until a worm damaged it. God used Jonah’s concern for the plant to ask why he should not care for Nineveh’s people and animals.

stories.title: Esther speaks up
stories.drawPrompt: Find the scepter in the picture. What might Esther be thinking as she approaches the king?

activity.prompt: What did Esther ask the Jews in Susa to do before she approached the king?
activity.explanation: Esther asked them to fast for her. She and her attendants would fast too.

paragraphs: Queen Esther learned that Haman had persuaded the king to order the destruction of the Jewish people. Mordecai told her about the order and asked her to plead for her people. Entering the king’s court uninvited could cost Esther her life.

Mordecai asked whether Esther had come to her royal position for such a time. She asked the Jews in Susa to fast with her for three days. Then she entered the court. When the king held out his gold scepter, she could speak safely.

Esther invited the king and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second one. There she asked the king to spare her life and the lives of her people. When the king asked who was responsible, Esther named Haman.

The danger did not end with Haman’s downfall. Esther pleaded with the king again because the original decree still stood. The king authorized a new decree that allowed the Jewish people to defend themselves.
middle.question: Where do you see Esther preparing carefully before she speaks up?

paragraphs: Haman secures an imperial decree against the Jewish people. Esther has access to the palace, but the law also restricts her access to the king. Mordecai challenges her assumption that royal status can shelter her from what threatens everyone else.

Mordecai frames the purpose of Esther’s position as a question. Esther responds by asking the community in Susa to fast with her before she acts. The text holds the uncertainty of the outcome alongside her decision to enter the court.

The king extends the scepter, and Esther uses two banquets to choose the moment for her appeal. When she reveals that her own life is threatened along with her people’s, the court must reckon with a decree it has already authorized.

Haman’s removal does not cancel the decree. Esther returns to plead again, and the king authorizes another order, written in his name, to allow the Jews to defend themselves. The story gives attention both to Esther’s personal courage and to the changes required to protect others.
teen.question: How does Esther’s use of timing and community support shape what courage looks like in this story?

paragraphs: King Darius trusted Daniel and planned to give him more responsibility. Other officials looked for wrongdoing but could not find any. They persuaded the king to sign a law saying that for thirty days people could make requests only to the king.

Daniel heard about the law and went home. He knelt by his upstairs windows, which opened toward Jerusalem, and prayed as usual. The officials reported him. Darius tried to rescue Daniel, but the law could not be changed, and Daniel was put into the lions’ den.

The worried king spent the night without food or sleep. At dawn he called into the den. Daniel answered that God had sent an angel to shut the lions’ mouths. When Daniel was pulled out, he had no injury.
middle.question: Why is it important that Daniel was already in the habit of praying before the law was signed?

paragraphs: Daniel’s rivals cannot find corruption or negligence in his work, so they target his religious practice. They tell Darius that officials agree on a temporary decree concentrating petitions on the king. The king signs it, giving political force to a plan he does not yet understand.

Daniel knows the decree has been signed. His posture, open windows toward Jerusalem, and daily schedule are described in familiar terms. When the officials accuse him, they use the very rule the king signed to argue that the king cannot save the official he trusts.

Darius seals the den and spends a sleepless night. At dawn Daniel credits his rescue to God, who sent an angel to shut the lions’ mouths. The encounter reverses the helplessness the king displayed the night before. The chapter ends with Darius addressing his kingdom about Daniel’s God.

activity.prompt: What surprised Moses about the bush?
options: It was on fire and stayed whole
activity.explanation: Moses turned aside because the fire did not burn up the bush.

paragraphs: Moses was looking after sheep. He led them through the wilderness to a mountain. There he saw a bush that was on fire. Even though he could see flames, the bush did not burn up. He came closer to look.
God called, ‘Moses! Moses!’ Moses answered that he was there. God told him to take off his sandals. The ground where Moses stood was holy. Moses covered his face.

God had seen how badly the Israelites were being treated in Egypt and had heard them cry for help. He told Moses to go to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and lead the people out. Moses wondered why he was the one to go.

God promised to be with Moses. Moses still had questions. He worried that he would have trouble speaking, so God told him that his brother Aaron could help. Moses had a hard job to do, and he had someone to go with him.
young.question: What help did God promise Moses when he was afraid to go?

paragraphs: Moses was tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro when he came to Horeb. A bush burned without being consumed. Moses turned aside to investigate, and God called him by name from the bush.
Moses answered, and God warned him to stop and remove his sandals because the ground was holy. God identified himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses hid his face.

God said he had seen the suffering of his people, heard their cries, and come to rescue them from Egypt. He commissioned Moses to go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out. When Moses asked who he was to do such a thing, God promised to go with him.

Moses continued to ask questions, including what he should say if the people asked for God’s name. In Exodus 4 he also raised his difficulty with speaking. God said Aaron would speak with him and that God would teach them what to do.
middle.question: How does God’s answer in Exodus 3:12 respond to Moses’ question in verse 11?

paragraphs: Exodus 3 opens with Moses keeping another person’s flock. The burning bush interrupts ordinary work, and the narrator notes that God calls after seeing Moses turn aside. Moses’ curiosity brings him to the edge of a place he is told is holy.

The instructions to stop and remove his sandals establish the seriousness of the encounter. God identifies himself in relation to Moses’ ancestors. Moses covers his face, and God begins speaking about the suffering of people in Egypt.

The movement from God seeing, hearing, and knowing the Israelites’ suffering to God sending Moses gives the commission its purpose. Moses questions his own standing. God responds with a promise of presence and a sign tied to what will happen after the people leave.

Moses asks what name he should give the Israelites. Later he doubts whether he can speak well enough. The conversation includes both resistance and practical help. Aaron is appointed to speak, and Moses still has a role in communicating the message.
teen.question: Compare Moses’ questions in Exodus 3:11 and 4:10. Which parts of God’s answers address Moses’ fear, and which still ask him to act?

stories.drawPrompt: Color a dry path through the water and draw footprints leading to the far shore.

activity.prompt: How did the Israelites get across the sea?
activity.explanation: God opened a path through the sea, and the Israelites walked across on dry ground.

paragraphs: The Israelites had left Egypt, where they had been forced to work. They camped near the sea. When they saw Pharaoh’s army coming after them, they were afraid. Moses told them to watch how God would rescue them.
God told the people to move forward. Moses stretched his hand over the sea. A strong wind blew through the night. The water parted, and the families walked across on dry ground.
Pharaoh’s army followed them into the path. After the Israelites crossed, the water came back. They were safe on the other side. The people saw what God had done and trusted him.
young.question: How do you think the families felt when they reached the other shore?

paragraphs: After the Israelites left Egypt, Pharaoh changed his mind and sent chariots after them. The Israelites were camped by the sea. They cried out and blamed Moses for bringing them there. Moses urged them to stand firm and see how the Lord would rescue them.

God directed the Israelites to go forward. The pillar of cloud moved behind them, separating their camp from the Egyptian army. Moses extended his hand, and an east wind drove back the sea all night. The people crossed on dry ground.

The chariots followed, but their wheels struggled. At dawn the waters returned, and the army was swept away. Exodus 14 ends with the people recognizing what God had done and putting their trust in the Lord and in Moses.
middle.question: How do Moses’ words in Exodus 14:13–14 and God’s instruction in verse 15 fit together?

paragraphs: Exodus 13 explains that the Israelites are led away from the shorter route and guided by the pillar of cloud and fire. When Pharaoh pursues them in chapter 14, the people question whether freedom has only led them into danger. Moses promises deliverance.

In the narrative God’s command to move forward comes alongside the promise that God will fight for the people. Moses stretches out his hand, the wind blows, and the pillar of cloud separates the camps. The passage gives attention both to God’s action and to the Israelites walking into the opened path.

The Egyptians pursue the Israelites and are overtaken by the returning water. The ending puts their defeat beside the Israelites’ rescue and the people’s response of awe and trust. The next chapter turns the event into a song the community can remember together.
teen.question: Compare the people’s response in Exodus 14:10–12 with 14:30–31. What changes and what does the narrator say led to the change?

activity.prompt: Who helped Samuel understand the voice?
activity.explanation: Eli understood that the Lord was calling Samuel and told him how to answer.

paragraphs: Samuel helped Eli serve God. One night Samuel lay down near the place where the lamp of God was still burning. He heard his name and ran to Eli. Eli said he had not called him.
Samuel heard his name again and went back to Eli. The third time, Eli understood that the Lord was calling the boy. He told Samuel to lie down and ask God to speak because he was listening.
The Lord called Samuel by name again. This time Samuel answered as Eli had taught him. God gave him a message, and Samuel listened. The next morning Samuel told Eli what he had heard.
young.question: What did Eli do to help Samuel listen?

paragraphs: Samuel served under Eli at the sanctuary. The writer says a word from the Lord was rare in those days. Before the lamp went out, Samuel heard his name and thought Eli needed him. Each time Samuel went to Eli, Eli sent him back to bed.
After the third call, Eli realized who was speaking. He taught Samuel to answer as a servant ready to listen. When the Lord called again, Samuel did as Eli had said.

The message concerned Eli’s household, and Samuel was afraid to repeat it. In the morning Eli asked him to tell everything, and Samuel did. As Samuel grew, the people came to recognize him as a prophet.
middle.question: How did Samuel show that he was willing to listen and tell the truth even when the message was hard?

paragraphs: The account opens with two details. A word from the Lord is rare, and the lamp of God has not yet gone out. Samuel hears a voice but interprets it through the relationship he already knows, getting up each time to serve Eli.
Eli eventually recognizes the speaker. His instruction gives Samuel a way to respond and a posture to take. Eli helps Samuel listen even though the message calls Eli’s own household to account.

In the morning Samuel fears telling Eli what he heard. Eli asks him to speak fully, and Samuel tells him the whole message. By the end of the chapter Samuel is recognized publicly as a prophet, beginning with the difficult act of telling the truth to his mentor.
teen.question: What do Eli and Samuel each do to make it possible for a difficult message to be heard?

activity.prompt: What did Zacchaeus climb to see Jesus?
activity.explanation: Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree so he could see above the crowd.

paragraphs: Jesus was passing through Jericho. A man named Zacchaeus wanted to see him. Zacchaeus was short, and the crowd was in the way. He ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree.
Jesus looked up and called Zacchaeus by name. He asked Zacchaeus to come down because he was going to stay at his house. Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed him happily.

Some people complained because Jesus was visiting a man they thought had done wrong. Zacchaeus offered to share his money with people in need and pay back anyone he had cheated. Jesus said he had come to find and save people who were lost.
young.question: What did Zacchaeus say he would do to make things right?

paragraphs: Zacchaeus was a wealthy chief tax collector in Jericho. When Jesus passed through, Zacchaeus could not see past the crowd. He ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree.
Jesus stopped below the tree, called him by name, and said he must stay at his house. Zacchaeus welcomed Jesus gladly, but the crowd grumbled that Jesus had chosen to be the guest of a sinner.

Zacchaeus told Jesus he would give half his possessions to the poor and repay anyone he had cheated four times what he had taken. Jesus spoke of salvation coming to the house. He ended by explaining that the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.
middle.question: What is the difference between sharing with the poor and paying someone back? Why do both matter in this story?

paragraphs: Luke names Zacchaeus’s wealth and position before describing his effort to see Jesus. Zacchaeus gets ahead of the crowd, but Jesus makes the encounter personal by looking up, naming him, and saying he will stay at his house.

The scene places Zacchaeus’s joyful welcome beside the crowd’s complaint. The crowd’s label sums up how it sees him, while Jesus’s willingness to enter his house makes room for an encounter beyond that reputation.

Zacchaeus names two concrete actions, giving to the poor and restoring fourfold what he has taken dishonestly. Jesus answers with a declaration of salvation and calls Zacchaeus a son of Abraham. The final verse explains the encounter in terms of Jesus’s mission to seek and save.
teen.question: How do Jesus’s welcome and Zacchaeus’s promises work together in the story? What would you miss by reading either part alone?

activity.prompt: What did the shepherd do when he found the sheep?
options: He put it on his shoulders
He put it on a boat
activity.explanation: The shepherd carried the sheep on his shoulders and invited others to celebrate.

paragraphs: People came to listen to Jesus. Some teachers complained because Jesus welcomed people who had done wrong. Jesus answered with a story.
A shepherd had one hundred sheep. When one was missing, he went looking for it. He kept searching until he found it. Then he put it on his shoulders and carried it home.
The shepherd was so happy that he asked his friends and neighbors to celebrate with him. Jesus said there is joy in heaven when someone turns back to God.
young.question: Why did the shepherd ask his neighbors to celebrate?

paragraphs: Tax collectors and others were gathering to hear Jesus. Some religious leaders complained that he welcomed and ate with people they called sinners. Jesus responded with a parable.

He asked what a person with one hundred sheep would do if one went missing. In the story the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine in the open country and searches until he finds the missing sheep. He carries it back on his shoulders, rejoicing.

At home the shepherd calls his friends and neighbors to share his joy. Jesus connects that celebration to the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. The ending answers the complaint about whom Jesus welcomes.
middle.question: How does the celebration at the end answer the complaint at the beginning?

paragraphs: Luke places the parable in a public disagreement about meals and welcome. Some hearers draw near to Jesus, while critics grumble that he eats with sinners. Jesus directs a question back to them about a lost sheep.

The search continues until the sheep is found. The shepherd’s response is to carry it home rejoicing. In a few lines the parable moves from the flock to the missing individual to a shared celebration with neighbors.

Jesus interprets the shepherd’s joy as joy in heaven over a sinner who repents. The story starts with a complaint about hospitality and ends with an invitation to rejoice. Its frame gives the listeners a choice about how to respond when someone is found.
teen.question: What does the shared celebration add to the parable’s answer to the people who grumbled?

activity.prompt: What did the wise builder build on?
activity.explanation: The house built on rock stood through the storm.

paragraphs: Jesus told a story about two builders. One built a house on a rock. The other built a house on sand.
Rain came down and water rose. The wind blew against both houses. The house on rock stayed up. The house on sand fell with a crash.
Jesus said that when we hear his words and do what they say, we are like the builder who built on rock. He wanted people to put his words into practice.
young.question: What did Jesus say a wise person does after hearing his words?

paragraphs: Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with two builders. The first represents someone who hears Jesus’s words and acts on them. That person is like a builder who sets a house on rock.
The second builder represents someone who hears the same words and does not act on them. That house is built on sand. Rain, floodwater, and wind hit both houses.
The house on rock stands, and the house on sand falls. The storm reveals what each builder chose before the rain began. The picture calls Jesus’s listeners to act on what they have heard.
middle.question: What do the two builders have in common, and what choice makes their houses turn out differently?

paragraphs: The illustration comes at the end of the Sermon on the Mount. Earlier in Matthew 7:21–23, Jesus distinguishes speaking the right words from doing the Father’s will. The building story gives the distinction a concrete picture.
The two people both hear Jesus. Both build, and both face rain, floods, and wind. The repeated description of the storm keeps the comparison centered on the foundation each person chose.

The house founded on rock withstands the storm, while the house on sand collapses. Matthew then describes the crowd’s astonishment at Jesus’s authority. The placement invites readers to consider what they will do with the teaching they just heard.
teen.question: Choose one teaching from Matthew 5–7. What would putting it into practice look like in an ordinary week?

stories.drawPrompt: Color the garden and draw another plant Adam and Eve could have cared for.

activity.prompt: What did Adam and Eve do when they heard God in the garden?
activity.explanation: They hid among the trees. God called out and asked where they were.

paragraphs: God put the man in a garden called Eden to work in it and care for it. God said he could eat from the garden’s trees, but gave him one tree to leave alone. God made a woman, and the man and woman lived in the garden together.

A serpent spoke to the woman and made her question what God had said. She took fruit from the tree God had told them to leave alone. She gave some to the man, and he ate too. When they heard God in the garden, they hid.
God called to them and asked what had happened. The man and the woman each pointed to someone else. They had to leave the garden. Before they went, God made clothes for them.
young.question: When something goes wrong, who is a trusted person you can talk to about it?

paragraphs: In Genesis 2, God sets the man in Eden to work and guard the garden. God gives wide permission to eat and draws one boundary at the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The chapter also says the man should have a partner, and the woman joins him there.

In Genesis 3, the serpent’s question reshapes what God said. The woman considers the fruit and eats, and the man eats some too. They realize they are exposed, make coverings, and hide. God calls to the man and asks what has happened.

The man points to the woman, and the woman points to the serpent. God describes the consequences of their choices. God makes garments for them and sends them out of Eden, setting a guard at the way to the tree of life.
middle.question: Compare Genesis 2:16–17 and 3:1. What part of God’s words does the serpent’s question leave out?

paragraphs: Genesis 2 frames human life in the garden around work, care, limits, and relationship. Permission to eat from the garden precedes the single prohibition. The account ends with the man and woman together and without shame.

In Genesis 3 the serpent’s question brings the prohibition to the foreground. After the man and woman eat, the story moves through covering, hiding, and blame. God’s questions draw out their actions and show what has changed in their relationships.

The consequences affect work, relationships, and access to the garden. The text places God’s act of clothing them before their departure. Eden closes to them, and life outside it still includes work and care.
teen.question: Where do you see trust giving way to hiding and blame? Which detail complicates a reading focused only on punishment?

activity.prompt: What happened when the people could no longer understand one another?
activity.explanation: The people stopped building the city and scattered across the earth.

paragraphs: Long ago, the people in this story all spoke the same language. They found a wide plain and settled there. They made bricks and baked them until they were hard.
The people wanted to build a city with a very tall tower. They thought it would make their name well known and keep everyone from scattering. They worked together on the tower.
God confused their language, and the builders could no longer understand one another. They stopped building the city and moved to different places. The city was called Babel.
young.question: How could you help someone understand you if they speak a different language?

paragraphs: Genesis 11 opens with the whole earth sharing one language. People settle on the plain of Shinar and make fired bricks, using bitumen to hold them together. Their shared speech and building methods make a large project possible.

They set out to build a city and a tower reaching toward the heavens. Their stated reasons are to make a name for themselves and to keep from being scattered. The narrator then describes the Lord coming down to see what they built.
The Lord confuses their language so they cannot understand one another. They stop building the city and scatter. Genesis connects the name Babel with the confusion of speech.
middle.question: Which of the builders’ stated goals is reversed at the end of the story?

paragraphs: The opening of Genesis 11 presents shared language, settlement, and technology. The repeated phrase inviting one another to act moves the people from making bricks to building a public monument. They name fame and remaining together as their goals.

Their tower is meant to reach the heavens, yet the narrator describes the Lord coming down to inspect it. The contrast in scale sits beside the Lord’s observation about what their unity allows them to attempt.

The confusion of speech stops the building, and the people experience the dispersal they wanted to prevent. Immediately after the genealogy that follows, Genesis 12 opens with God calling Abram away from his home and promising to make his name great.
teen.question: Compare Genesis 11:4 and 12:2–3. How are the goals and beneficiaries of a great name presented in each passage?

activity.prompt: Who went with Abram when he left Haran?
activity.explanation: Abram took Sarai and Lot, along with the people and possessions of his household.

paragraphs: Before people called him Abraham, his name was Abram. God told Abram to leave his home and go to a land God would show him. God promised to bless Abram and said that other families would be blessed through him too.
Abram set out from Haran with his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot. They took their things and the people traveling with them. They traveled until they reached the land of Canaan.
At Shechem, God promised the land to Abram’s family after him. Abram built an altar to worship God. The family moved on and pitched their tents again. The journey kept going.
young.question: What could help you trust someone who is leading you to a place you have never seen?

paragraphs: God calls Abram to leave his country, relatives, and father’s household for a land God will show him. God promises to make a nation from him, bless him, and give him a great name. All the families of the earth are named in the blessing.

Abram leaves Haran at seventy-five. Sarai and Lot travel with him, along with their household and possessions. They reach Canaan and stop at Shechem, where the Lord appears and speaks about giving the land to Abram’s descendants.

Abram builds an altar at Shechem, then moves between Bethel and Ai, pitches his tent, and builds another altar. The chapter shows both travel and worship as Abram follows the call. Later Genesis uses the names Abraham and Sarah.
middle.question: Who besides Abram is meant to benefit from the blessing in Genesis 12:1–3?

paragraphs: At the end of Genesis 11, Terah’s household sets out toward Canaan and settles in Haran instead. The following chapter opens with a call to Abram to leave familiar ties and go to a land God will show him. Promise comes before the path is fully described.

God promises Abram a great name and a people, but the promises reach beyond his household. The passage connects his blessing with all the families of the earth. Abram goes with Sarai, Lot, and the people and possessions of his household.

At Shechem the land is promised to Abram’s descendants, and Abram marks the encounter with an altar. The second altar between Bethel and Ai continues that pattern. Tent and altar mark a life in motion with deliberate places of worship.
teen.question: Compare the things Abram is asked to leave with the people included in the promise. How does each list shape your reading of the journey?

stories.title: Sarah Laughs
stories.drawPrompt: Color Sarah’s shawl and the tent. Draw a detail that shows there is reason to celebrate.

activity.prompt: What name did Abraham and Sarah give their son?
activity.explanation: They named their son Isaac. His name is linked to laughter.

paragraphs: Abraham was sitting by his tent when three visitors came. He welcomed them and brought food. Sarah helped get the meal ready.
One of the visitors said Sarah would have a son. Sarah heard the promise from the tent and laughed quietly. Abraham and Sarah were old, and the news seemed impossible to her.
Later Sarah had a baby, just as God had promised. Abraham named him Isaac. Sarah said God had brought her laughter, and other people would laugh with her. This time the laughter went with joy.
young.question: How does Sarah’s laughter change from the first part of the story to the last?

paragraphs: In Genesis 18, three visitors arrive near Abraham’s tent. Abraham offers water and a meal, and Sarah prepares bread. After the meal the visitors ask where Sarah is, then one says she will have a son when he returns.

Sarah listens at the tent entrance and laughs to herself. She and Abraham are advanced in years, which makes the promise hard to believe. The Lord asks why she laughed and whether anything is too hard for him.

Genesis 21 says the Lord did for Sarah what he had promised. Abraham names the child Isaac. Sarah speaks of the laughter God has given her and expects others to share it. The same action now expresses a different response to the promise.
middle.question: What is Sarah responding to when she laughs in Genesis 18:12, and what is she responding to in 21:6?

paragraphs: Genesis 17 records Abraham laughing when God says Sarah will have a son. God gives the child’s name as Isaac. In Genesis 18 the promise comes again in the setting of hospitality, after Abraham and Sarah prepare food for visitors.

Sarah overhears the promise and laughs to herself. The narrator names the reason the promise is hard to imagine. The Lord’s question about what is too hard places Sarah’s immediate assessment beside divine ability.

Genesis 21 repeats that God acted as promised. Sarah describes laughter as something God has given her and anticipates other people laughing with her. The story moves from private astonishment to joy she can share publicly.
teen.question: Compare Abraham’s laughter in Genesis 17:17 with Sarah’s in 18:12 and 21:6. What changes over those three moments?

stories.drawPrompt: Color the brothers’ robes and draw the path where Esau ran to meet Jacob.

activity.prompt: What did Esau do when he saw Jacob?
activity.explanation: Esau ran to meet Jacob, hugged him, and wept with him.

paragraphs: Jacob and Esau were brothers. Long before, Jacob had tricked their father to get a blessing meant for Esau. After many years away, Jacob came back and heard that Esau was coming to meet him. Jacob was afraid.
Jacob prayed and sent gifts ahead. That night, Jacob was alone after his family crossed a stream. He wrestled until dawn, and he was given a new name, Israel.
In the morning, Jacob bowed as he came near Esau. Esau ran to meet him and hugged him. Both brothers cried. Jacob urged Esau to accept his gift, and Esau did. They went on their journeys in peace.
young.question: What did Esau do that surprised Jacob after he had been afraid?

paragraphs: Jacob is returning after years away from Esau. Their last time together ended with anger over Isaac’s blessing. When Jacob hears that Esau is coming with four hundred men, he divides his camp, prays for rescue, and sends ahead a series of gifts.
Jacob sends his household across the Jabbok and is left alone. A man wrestles with him until daybreak. Jacob receives a blessing and a new name, Israel. He leaves the encounter limping.

Jacob bows seven times as he approaches his brother. Esau runs to him, embraces him, and weeps with him. After Jacob urges him to receive the gift, Esau accepts it. The brothers talk about traveling and then head toward different places.
middle.question: How do Jacob’s plans in Genesis 32 compare with what actually happens in Genesis 33:4?

paragraphs: Jacob approaches Esau expecting danger. He divides his camp, recalls God’s promise in prayer, and sends gifts ahead. The preparations show how deeply the conflict over Isaac’s blessing still shapes what he expects.

After the family crosses the Jabbok, the account interrupts the expected meeting with a night of wrestling. Jacob receives the name Israel and leaves with a limp. The next scene begins with him looking up and seeing Esau.

Esau’s run and embrace interrupt Jacob’s careful approach. Jacob urges Esau to accept his gift and compares seeing his brother’s face with seeing the face of God. Their exchange ends with acceptance and separate routes, giving the reconciliation a quieter conclusion than Jacob anticipates.
teen.question: How does the reference to seeing Esau’s face in Genesis 33:10 connect the meeting with the night before?

stories.title: Baby Moses in the Basket
stories.drawPrompt: Color the reeds and draw gentle ripples around the basket.

activity.prompt: Who found the basket by the river?
activity.explanation: Pharaoh’s daughter saw the basket, had it brought to her, and felt compassion for the baby.

paragraphs: In Egypt, the ruler gave a cruel order that put Hebrew baby boys in danger. One mother hid her baby for three months. When she could hide him no longer, she made a basket that would keep water out. She put it among the reeds by the river.

The baby’s sister stayed nearby to see what would happen. Pharaoh’s daughter came to the river and saw the basket. A servant brought it to her. When the princess opened it and heard the baby cry, she felt sorry for him.

The baby’s sister offered to find someone to care for him. She brought his own mother. His mother cared for him until he grew older. Then Pharaoh’s daughter took him into her family and called him Moses.
young.question: What did each person do to help keep the baby safe?

paragraphs: Exodus 1 ends with Pharaoh ordering Hebrew sons to be thrown into the Nile. In the next chapter, a Levite mother hides her child for three months. When she can no longer hide him, she coats a papyrus basket and sets it among the reeds along the river.
His sister watches from a distance. Pharaoh’s daughter notices the basket, sends a servant to get it, and opens it. She recognizes the crying baby as a Hebrew child and has compassion on him.

The sister offers to find a Hebrew woman to nurse him and brings his mother. Pharaoh’s daughter pays her to care for him. When he is older, she takes him as her son, naming him Moses because she drew him out of the water.
middle.question: Which choices in Exodus 2:1–10 change what Pharaoh’s order would have meant for the baby?

paragraphs: The story follows Pharaoh’s command about the Nile in Exodus 1:22. The basket uses the same river as a place to protect a child. Details about the coating, reeds, and watching sister make the mother’s decision both deliberate and uncertain.

Pharaoh’s daughter recognizes the child as Hebrew. Her compassion becomes a decision to protect someone endangered by her own household’s authority. The sister sees a chance to speak and offers a practical way to care for the baby.

The mother receives the child back as his nurse, and Pharaoh’s daughter later adopts and names him. The chapter opens Moses’s story through the actions of the women who help him survive, long before Moses acts on behalf of his people.
teen.question: How do the women use the choices available to them, and where does their cooperation cross the boundaries Pharaoh tried to impose?

stories.drawPrompt: Color the manger and draw a detail that would help the shepherds know they had found the right place.

activity.prompt: What helped the shepherds know they had found Jesus?
options: A baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger
activity.explanation: The angel told them to look for a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger.

paragraphs: The ruler called for people to be counted. Joseph traveled with Mary to Bethlehem. While they were there, Mary gave birth to Jesus. She wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger because there was no room for them in the guest room.

Nearby, shepherds were watching their sheep at night. An angel told them to be unafraid and brought good news of great joy. A Savior had been born. They would find a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger.

The shepherds hurried to Bethlehem. They found Mary, Joseph, and the baby, just as they had been told. They shared the news and went back praising God. Mary kept these things in her heart and thought about them.
young.question: How did the shepherds share their joy after they saw the baby?

paragraphs: Luke begins with a decree for registration. Joseph travels from Nazareth to Bethlehem because he belongs to David’s family. Mary gives birth there, wraps the child, and lays him in a manger because the guest room has no space for them.

The announcement comes to shepherds working outside at night. The angel tells them a Savior, the Christ and Lord, has been born in David’s town. The sign is a wrapped infant in a manger. A multitude praises God and announces peace.

The shepherds go to see what the Lord has made known. They find the sign and tell others what they heard. Their hearers are amazed, Mary ponders what has happened, and the shepherds return praising God.
middle.question: Why might the manger be an unexpected sign after the angel’s announcement in Luke 2:10–12?

paragraphs: Luke places the birth within a ruler’s decree reaching across the empire. The registration brings Joseph and Mary to the city of David. The birth itself is described through spare details about wrapping the child, a manger, and a lack of space.

The angel uses expansive language about joy, a Savior, and peace, then gives the shepherds a specific sign. The language of the announcement sits alongside a newborn in a feeding trough. The shepherds travel to see whether what they heard matches what they find.

Luke gives different responses to the same news. The shepherds speak and praise, their hearers are amazed, and Mary keeps and ponders what happened. The story moves from rulers issuing orders to workers carrying news and a mother holding it in memory.
teen.question: How does Luke’s movement from the emperor’s decree to the shepherds’ report shape who matters in the story?

stories.topic: Belovedness and the beginning of Jesus’ ministry

activity.prompt: What did the Spirit descend like?
activity.explanation: Matthew describes the Spirit of God coming down like a dove.

paragraphs: John was baptizing people in the Jordan River. Jesus came from Galilee and asked John to baptize him. John was surprised and said that he needed to be baptized by Jesus.
Jesus told John to go ahead because it was right for them to do this. John agreed and baptized Jesus in the Jordan.
As Jesus came up from the water, the heavens opened. The Spirit came down like a dove. A voice from heaven said that Jesus was his beloved Son and that he was pleased with him.
young.question: What did the voice from heaven tell us about Jesus?

paragraphs: Jesus travels from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized. John objects, saying Jesus ought to baptize him. Jesus asks him to allow it for now so they can fulfill all righteousness, and John agrees.
Jesus comes up from the water, and the scene moves from their conversation to the opened heavens. Matthew describes the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on Jesus.
A voice from heaven calls Jesus his beloved Son and expresses delight in him. The account appears just before Jesus goes into the wilderness and begins to teach publicly.
middle.question: What do John’s words and the heavenly voice each say about who Jesus is?

paragraphs: Matthew has introduced John as a wilderness preacher calling hearers to repentance. John distinguishes his baptism with water from the work of one coming after him. When Jesus asks for baptism, John’s objection puts that difference into words.

Jesus responds with the language of fulfilling righteousness. John consents. Matthew then concentrates the scene around three actions: Jesus rises from the water, the heavens open, and the Spirit descends like a dove.

The voice identifies Jesus as the beloved Son and expresses God’s pleasure in him. The declaration comes before the wilderness and the public work that follows. It gives readers a statement about Jesus’s identity before they watch what he does next.
teen.question: Why does it matter that this declaration comes before the testing in the wilderness and Jesus’s public ministry?

stories.title: Jesus Calls the First Disciples
stories.topic: Following, learning, and a new purpose
stories.drawPrompt: Color the fishing boat and draw what the brothers left on the shore when they followed Jesus.

activity.prompt: What were Simon and Andrew doing when Jesus called them?
activity.explanation: Simon and Andrew were casting a net into the Sea of Galilee because they were fishermen.

paragraphs: Jesus came to Galilee and told people good news about God’s kingdom. As he walked beside the lake, he saw two brothers, Simon and Andrew. They were throwing a net into the water to catch fish.
Jesus invited them to follow him. He said he would teach them to fish for people. They left their nets and went with him.
A little farther on, Jesus saw James and John fixing their nets in a boat. He called them too. They left the boat with their father and the workers and went after Jesus.
young.question: What did the brothers do when Jesus told them to follow him?

paragraphs: After John is arrested, Jesus comes to Galilee announcing that God’s kingdom has come near. Beside the lake he sees Simon, later called Peter, and Andrew casting nets as part of their work.
Jesus calls them to follow and tells them he will make them fishers of people. The invitation uses the work they already know as a picture of something new. They leave the nets immediately.

Jesus then calls James and John while they mend nets in a boat. They leave their father Zebedee with the hired workers and follow. Mark tells both calls side by side so readers can notice what repeats and what changes.
middle.question: How does Jesus use familiar work to describe a new purpose?

paragraphs: Mark places the calls directly after Jesus’s announcement about the nearness of God’s kingdom. Simon and Andrew are working with a net when Jesus makes the invitation. The account gives no long discussion between the call and their response.
The promise to make them fishers of people takes language from their current lives. Their departure leaves behind tools of their trade. The words also describe what Jesus will make of them over time.

The second pair is described through relationships and responsibilities inside a boat. James and John leave Zebedee with hired workers. The two accounts emphasize an immediate response while leaving room for the rest of Mark to show what following Jesus entails.
teen.question: What stays connected to the fishermen’s old lives, and what changes when they follow Jesus?
